name: The Recurring Null

stars.name: Iterance
stars.notes: Old, dim K-dwarf. The star itself is unremarkable. The signal originates from its fourth planet, not the star.

planets.name: Static
planets.notes: Innermost world at 0.1 AU. Tidally locked. The sunlit hemisphere emits a faint, continuous radio hiss that does not correspond to any thermal or geological process.

planets.name: Reverberation
planets.notes: Orbits at 0.35 AU. Seismic activity follows a pattern that exactly mirrors the signal from the fourth planet, delayed by 11.4 minutes—the light-travel time between the two worlds.

planets.name: Lacuna
planets.notes: Dead world at 0.7 AU. No atmosphere, no geological activity. Surface is perfectly smooth to millimeter resolution across 30% of the southern hemisphere—an impossibility for a natural body.

planets.name: The Transmitter
planets.notes: Ice world at 1.8 AU. Source of a powerful, structured radio signal that has been broadcasting continuously for at least 340 years based on light-cone analysis. No surface features or subsurface structures have been identified as the signal source.

anomalies.name: The Signal
anomalies.notes: A complex, structured radio transmission broadcasting at 1.42 GHz (hydrogen line) with 73 distinct modulation patterns. The signal repeats on a 71-hour cycle. It is clearly artificial but encodes no recognizable language, mathematics, or data structure. Every attempt at decryption has failed. The signal has been active for at least 340 years.

anomalies.name: The Smooth Surface
anomalies.notes: Thirty percent of Lacuna's southern hemisphere has been polished smooth to millimeter precision. No erosion process can achieve this uniformity on a world with no atmosphere. The boundary between smoothed and unsmoothed terrain is a perfect geometric curve—a section of a logarithmic spiral.

anomalies.name: The Seismic Echo
anomalies.notes: Seismic activity on Reverberation mirrors the modulation pattern of The Signal, delayed by exactly the light-travel time between the two worlds. The planet's interior is responding to a radio transmission as if it were a receiver. No mechanism for this coupling is known.

faction_control.notes: The system is flagged in SETI databases but has not been claimed by any faction. Its remoteness and the undeciphered nature of the signal have limited interest to academic circles.

history: The Signal was first detected in 2488 by the deep-space radio telescope array at Meridian Station. Its artificial nature was confirmed within hours, triggering a priority investigation.

A flyby mission in 2501 mapped the system and discovered the smooth surface on Lacuna and the seismic echo on Reverberation. The mission also confirmed that the signal originates from The Transmitter but found no surface or subsurface structure that could produce it.

Decryption efforts have been continuous since 2488. Over 200 research teams across known space have attempted to decode The Signal. None have succeeded. In 2530, cryptanalyst Dr. Yeun Park published a paper arguing that The Signal is not encrypted communication but rather the operational output of a machine—that it is not a message at all, but the sound of something running.
description: The Recurring Null is a dim K-dwarf system at the far edge of surveyed space, home to four unremarkable worlds and one very remarkable signal. The Transmitter, an ice world in the outer system, has been broadcasting a complex radio transmission on the hydrogen line for at least 340 years. The signal is structured, repetitive, and clearly artificial, but every attempt to decode it has failed. It plays on a 71-hour cycle, never varying, never stopping, a message—or a mechanism—operating in silence at the edge of nothing.

The system's other anomalies suggest the signal is not isolated. Reverberation, the second planet, experiences seismic activity that mirrors the signal's modulation pattern with a delay equal to the light-travel time between the two worlds—as if the planet's interior is receiving and responding to the transmission. Lacuna, the third planet, has had 30% of its southern hemisphere polished to millimeter smoothness by an unknown process, the boundary following a perfect logarithmic spiral. Static, the innermost world, emits its own continuous radio hiss. The system behaves less like a collection of planets and more like a collection of components.

The central question is not what The Signal says but what it does. Dr. Park's hypothesis—that it is operational output rather than communication—reframes the entire system as a machine. If correct, The Transmitter is the broadcaster, Reverberation is a resonator, Lacuna's smooth surface is a reflector or antenna, and Static provides background noise for calibration. The machine's purpose is unknown. It may be a beacon, a sensor, a weapon, or something with no human analog. Answering the question requires physical investigation: landing on The Transmitter to find the signal source, drilling into Reverberation to understand the seismic coupling, and analyzing Lacuna's surface to determine what process could polish a planet. The machine has been running for centuries. Understanding it could be the most important discovery in human history—or the most dangerous.
